Prevention: Tillage or pull out weeds before planting.
Mulch with a 15 to 20 cm (6 to 8 `) thick layer of non-tomato, non-potato plant rests (e.g. hay or tree leaves) after tomato transplanting at dry weather.
Crop rotation reduces weeds because certain weeds prefer to grow in certain crops.
The more different the crops are from tomato (e.g. maize, cabbages, beans) the better.
Irish potatoes, egg plants, peppers, nightshade, are less good for rotation with tomatoes because similar weeds grow in them.
Monitoring: There might be a number of non-tomato weedy plants in a tomato field.
If they become too abundant and/or grow higher than the tomato plants, then they hinder the tomato growth.
Non-tomato weedy plants often grow faster than tomatoes, and therefore early control is advised.
Weeds compete with tomatoes for soil nutrients and light.
Some long-flowering weeds can however attract and promote natural enemies which then attack tomato pests like aphids or whiteflies.
In case that weeds seriously outnumber tomato plants, particularly young plants, action might be considered.
Direct Control: Conduct mechanical/ manual weeding, particularly in young tomato fields.
Avoid weeding tomato fields that are attacked by fungal or bacterial diseases, to prevent transport of diseases from one plant to the next.
Do not weed during wet weather or in the morning, when plants are still moist, because potential diseases can be transported from one plant to the next.
Glyphosate herbicides ( Elglysate, Glycel, Gugukill, Gugusate, JembeSupa, Mamba, Mocphosate, Rondo, Rondopa, Sapikill
Touchall, Weedex, Willosate, and others) are applied before emergence of tomatoes.
Oxyfluorfen herbicides (Target, Boxyfan, Oxyfen, Sufen, and others) against broad leaf and annual grassy weeds.
Mainly a pre-emergence herbicide sprayed on moist fields (rain, irrigation) before tomato planting, or later carefully between rows of tomatoes.

No herbicides are permitted in integrated production, because they are too dangerous to farmers
consumers and the environment, and because mechanical control is effective and usually practical in tomato production.
In conventional farming a number of herbicides are available against broad- leaf weeds in tomatoes (mainly pre-emergence products) and against grasses.
Many are hazardous. and they should only be considered in exceptional cases.
When using a pesticide, always wear protective clothing and follow the instructions on the product label.
